title: Первый или второй?  (Track One or Track Two?)

segments.t: It is late at a small railway station. Anna is looking for the last train to Moscow. Boris knows the station, but tonight the departure board is wrong. Listen to their conversation in Russian.
Извините, это поезд в Москву?
Нет, ваш поезд на втором пути.
Но на табло написано: первый путь.
Табло не работает. Сегодня всё наоборот.
Подождите, это ваш чемодан?
Мой. А где мой билет?
У вас в руке.
Точно. Хорошо, что вы здесь.
Now listen again, one line at a time, with the meaning in English.
Извините, это поезд в Москву?
'Excuse me, is this the train to Moscow?' The first word means 'excuse me'. It gets a stranger's attention politely. The little word before Moscow means 'to': she is asking about a destination.
Нет, ваш поезд на втором пути.
'No, your train is on track two.' The word for 'train' comes back here. Listen for the phrase meaning 'on the second track'. At a station, the word for 'path' also means a railway track.
Но на табло написано: первый путь.

'But the board says: track one.' Her first word means 'but'. She has a reason to disagree. The last two words mean 'first track', and the word for 'first' is different from the word for 'second' you just heard.
Табло не работает. Сегодня всё наоборот.

'The board is not working. Today everything is the other way round.' Put the little word meaning 'not' before 'works' and you have 'is not working'. The final word means 'the other way round'. Boris is making a small joke about the confusion.
Подождите, это ваш чемодан?
'Wait, is this your suitcase?' The opening word means 'wait', said politely. She uses the same word for 'your' that Boris used earlier. This time it is his suitcase, not her train.
Мой. А где мой билет?
'Mine. And where is my ticket?' The short word repeated twice means 'my' or 'mine'. The question word means 'where'. A ticket is the thing he needs before he can get on the train.
У вас в руке.
'In your hand.' Russian describes this as 'at you, in the hand'. The phrase at the beginning means 'you have' in many everyday sentences. Here she is simply pointing out where his ticket is.
Точно. Хорошо, что вы здесь.

'Right. It is a good thing you are here.' The first word can mean 'exactly' or 'right'. The final word means 'here'. Boris helped Anna find her train, and now she has helped him find what he was holding all along.
Listen to the whole conversation once more. Can you catch the two track numbers, and where the missing ticket is?
Извините, это поезд в Москву?
Нет, ваш поезд на втором пути.
Но на табло написано: первый путь.
Табло не работает. Сегодня всё наоборот.
Подождите, это ваш чемодан?
Мой. А где мой билет?
У вас в руке.
Точно. Хорошо, что вы здесь.
A broken board sent Anna to the wrong track. Boris knew the way, but needed help finding his own ticket. Try listening once more without reading the translation.
До свидания!
